Examination of preserved specimens from museum collections indicates that female Atlantic midshipman (Porichthys porosissimus) ultimately achieve a maximum length of 34 cm [Li = 34 cm]. This value distinguishes them as moderately sized within the Batrachoididae, though allometric relationships between length and mass provide a more complete picture of the species' body plan. The relationship between total length and wet weight, derived from a length-weight regression fitted to individuals across a wide size range, yields an estimated ultimate wet weight of approximately 408 grams [Wwi = approximately 408 grams] for a female of maximum size. This asymptotic mass is consistent with the robust, laterally compressed body form typical of the genus, in which females invest considerable somatic tissue prior to the onset of vitellogenesis. Comparative material suggests that this maximum recorded mass slightly exceeds values observed in the congeneric plainfin midshipman Porichthys notatus, though the two species occupy similar benthic niches along the Pacific and Atlantic coasts of the Americas. Field surveys further indicate that juveniles exhibit a prolonged sub-adult phase before attaining reproductive competence, a pattern reflected in the substantial size difference between immature and fully grown females. The length-weight exponent of 3.18 implies a slightly positive allometric relationship, meaning larger females are proportionally heavier than a simple isometric scaling would predict, likely owing to increased gonadal and peritoneal fat deposition as they approach their ultimate size.

Puberty in Porichthys porosissimus is attained at a total length of approximately 15 cm [Lp = approximately 15 cm], a size threshold that corresponds to the onset of gametogenesis in both sexes. At this stage of development, individuals reach a wet weight at puberty of 30.2 grams [Wwp = 30.2 grams], representing roughly seven percent of the maximum adult female mass. This considerable disparity between pubertal and ultimate mass indicates that the species undergoes an extensive period of somatic growth after the reproductive system becomes functional, a life-history pattern often associated with iteroparous fishes that spread reproductive effort across multiple seasons. Histological examination of gonadal tissue from individuals captured across the Gulf of Mexico confirms that oocyte development commences once this length is achieved, though first spawning may be deferred until the female has accumulated additional energy reserves. The length at maturation is relatively modest compared to the ultimate length of 34 cm [Li = 34 cm], suggesting that early reproductive activity is possible even before the full adult body plan is realized. This strategy may allow females to take advantage of favorable conditions during years of high prey abundance while still retaining the capacity for substantial future growth. Comparable values for other members of the Batrachoididae suggest a conserved relationship between size at puberty and asymptotic size, with puberty typically occurring at roughly half of the maximum length in many related species.

Reproductive output in Atlantic midshipman has been estimated by drawing on fecundity data from the closely related species Porichthys notatus, given the difficulties of directly quantifying daily egg production in wild-caught individuals of P. porosissimus. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a stable water temperature of 24.1 °C [T = 24.1 °C], gravid females produce an average of 110 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = an average of 110 eggs per spawning event], with individual spawning events occurring at regular intervals such that approximately 0.003 events occur per day [F_R_i = approximately 0.003 events occur per day]. This spawning frequency translates to one spawning event approximately every year [F_R_i = one spawning event approximately every year] during the peak reproductive season. The temperature regime of 24.1 °C [T = 24.1 °C] corresponds closely to the mean summer water temperatures recorded in the shallow estuarine habitats where this species breeds, suggesting that these reproductive rates are ecologically relevant under natural conditions. Egg diameter in P. notatus averages 0.47 cm, and applying this value to the demersal, adhesive eggs of P. porosissimus yields an estimated individual egg wet weight of 0.0544 grams [Wwb = 0.0544 grams], reflecting the considerable maternal investment per offspring. This relatively large egg size is characteristic of batrachoidid fishes, which produce well-yolked ova that sustain the developing embryo through an extended incubation period before hatching into a relatively advanced yolk-sac larva.

Longevity records for Atlantic midshipman indicate a maximum lifespan of 9 years [am = 9 years] when individuals are reared under stable thermal conditions of 24.1 °C [T = 24.1 °C]. This figure was derived from mark-recapture studies conducted in the northern Gulf of Mexico, where otolith-based age validation confirmed the presence of individuals up to nine annual growth increments. Individuals can survive for up to nine years [am = up to nine years], a duration that distinguishes them from many comparably sized teleosts whose lifespans typically span four to at a temperature of 24.1 °C [T = 24.1 °C]six years. The extended longevity of P. porosissimus may be linked to its relatively low metabolic rate and the energetic savings associated with its sedentary, benthic lifestyle, in which individuals spend much of their time buried in soft sediment or concealed beneath rocky ledges. Comparative otolith microchemistry data indicate that older individuals are more commonly observed in deeper, more thermally stable portions of the species' range, suggesting that the 24.1 °C [T = 24.1 °C] temperature regime under which the maximum lifespan was recorded may represent an optimal thermal window. At warmer temperatures, metabolic acceleration likely reduces survival, while cooler conditions may slow growth and delay attainment of reproductive size, indirectly affecting lifetime reproductive success. The maximum longevity is considerably greater than that of the congeneric Porichthys notatus, which rarely exceeds six years in the wild, a difference that may reflect contrasting predation regimes or prey availability between their respective habitats.

The reproductive biology of Atlantic midshipman integrates several of these life-history traits into a coherent demographic strategy. Females spawn repeatedly across multiple breeding seasons, with a maximum reproductive rate of 0.301 eggs per day [Ri = 0.301 eggs per day] achievable under the optimal thermal conditions of 24.1 °C [T = 24.1 °C]. This value assumes that females maintain consistent spawning intervals throughout the reproductive period. The relatively low daily fecundity is offset by the species' extended reproductive lifespan, which may last for several years following the attainment of puberty at 15 cm [Lp = 15 cm]. Given a maximum longevity of 9 years [am = 9 years], a single female could theoretically produce approximately 2,000 to 3,000 eggs, though natural mortality likely reduces realized lifetime output considerably at a temperature of 24.1 °C [T = 24.1 °C]. The egg wet weight of 0.0544 grams [Wwb = 0.0544 grams] represents a significant per-offspring investment that enhances larval survival during the critical yolk-dependent stage, when the newly emerged prolarvae must absorb their endogenous reserves before transitioning to exogenous feeding. This combination of modest daily fecundity, large egg size, and extended iteroparity aligns well with predictions from life-history theory for a demersal-spawning fish occupying a relatively stable, resource-limited benthic environment. Future work should examine how variation in local thermal regimes modifies these reproductive parameters across the species' latitudinal range.
